title: The prayer settles in
hookLine: after long practice, the pilgrim finds the prayer running on its own with his heartbeat
tomorrow: what do you give when your hands are empty?

lines: A RHYTHM THAT NEVER NEEDS A REMINDER.
HE WAKES, AND IT'S ALREADY GOING.
cards: There's a rhythm in your chest that kept going through every class, every argument, every night of sleep, and never once needed a reminder. The pilgrim in The Way of a Pilgrim learns to set a prayer to that beat.
It doesn't start there. At first it's work. He says the Jesus Prayer over and over, as his elder told him, and some days it's dull; his tongue keeps going while his mind wanders off.
Then one morning he wakes, and the prayer is already going, before he's decided to start.

teach.h: FROM THE LIPS TO THE HEART.
teach.b: The elder gives him a daily task, and he keeps it: Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me, on the road, at meals, in the evening. After a while, he says, the prayer starts to move. It begins on his lips.
Then it seems to slip down into his heart.
Later, reading the Philokalia, he learns a way to join the words to his heartbeat, one word to each beat. Lord on one. Jesus on the next.
Christ on the next. And to let the words ride the breath, in and out. Then comes the part this lesson is named for.
The prayer, he says, seemed to pray by itself. It went on while he walked, while he talked with people, even, he says, while he slept.

teach.h: I SLEEP, BUT MY HEART WAKETH.
teach.b: Here's a line to tell a friend tonight, from the Song of Songs, that fits his picture: “I sleep, but my heart waketh.” The body rests; something underneath keeps watch. It's worth saying what the book doesn't promise.
It never calls this quick. He learned it under an elder's guidance, and some Orthodox teachers warn against forcing breath or heartbeat methods alone.
The prayer settles in the way a path gets worn into a field: by walking it, again and again, until the feet find it on their own.

how: Some Orthodox Christians pray the Jesus Prayer slowly with a prayer rope, sometimes in time with the breath, ideally with guidance from an experienced spiritual father or mother.

games.q: what does “the prayer settles in” mean?
o: a repeated prayer that, with practice, seems to pray itself
the moment a monk takes his final vows in a chapel
a prayer said only once at dawn, then set aside for the day

games.q: where the prayer goes — tap the pairs.
p: I sleep, but my heart waketh

s: the Jesus Prayer is a sound for emptying the mind
it's words spoken to someone: Lord Jesus Christ, have mercy on me.
the pilgrim says the prayer came easily from the start
at first it was work, even dull. only later did it seem to go on by itself.
the pilgrim says the prayer went on even while he slept
and the Song of Songs has a line that fits: I sleep, but my heart waketh.

games.q: your friend saw a video about syncing a prayer to your heartbeat and wants to master it this weekend, alone. what does the pilgrim's story suggest?
o: go for it; with enough focus it can be learned in a weekend.
start small and slow, and some teachers say: with someone to guide you.
skip it; methods like that are only meant for monks.
games.why: the pilgrim learned over a long time, under an elder's guidance, and some Orthodox teachers warn against forcing breath or heartbeat methods alone.

practice: Find your pulse, at the wrist or the side of the neck, or rest a hand flat on your chest until you feel the beat. Don't change it; just follow it. The pilgrim set Lord, Jesus, Christ on three beats.
You can do the same, or simply count the beats in threes, and let your breath go at its own pace.

wordCard.voice: The prayer settles in. Said again and again, until it moves from the lips to the heart and seems to go on by itself.

orig.note: Greek for 'have mercy', the heart of the Jesus Prayer, as in Kyrie eleison.

carryVoice: Pocket this one: the prayer prays itself. He didn't start there; he started with work. Day sixteen seventy, done.
